intro.label: Before Puppy Comes Home
intro.heading: What do you need before bringing home a Lhasa Apso puppy?
intro.html:
Before your Lhasa Apso puppy arrives, three things deserve specific attention: getting grooming tools and a plan in place (because the coat starts needing management early), knowing about renal dysplasia monitoring (so you don't miss early signs), and having pet insurance set up before the first vet visit (so nothing is excluded as pre-existing). The gear list matters, but these three items matter more.

This guide contains affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, Wooffy earns from qualifying purchases.

Essential Gear Checklist

  • Small to medium crate (24–30 inch) with divider
  • Soft dog bed or crate mat
  • Stainless steel food and water bowls (stainless is preferred over plastic to reduce bacterial buildup that can contribute to tear staining)
  • Flat collar + ID tag (engrave immediately)
    One option: GoTags Personalized Stainless Steel ID Tag on Amazon. An engraved stainless steel ID tag; you pick the shape and the lines of text at checkout. Put a phone number that's actually answered on it, and update the engraving if you move.
  • Harness for walks — distributes pressure safely for a small dog
  • 4–6 ft leash
  • Pin brush — the primary tool for the long coat
    One option: Chris Christensen Oval Pin Brush (27 mm) on Amazon. Chris Christensen's Original Series oval pin brush: 27 mm stainless pins without ball tips in a cushioned pad, made for long, silky and double coats. Brush in layers from the skin out; a pin brush is for daily maintenance, not for working out mats.
  • Slicker brush — useful for finishing and shorter puppy coat stages
    One option: Chris Christensen Big G Slicker Brush on Amazon. The Big G has long, angled pins set in a flexible cushioned pad, built for working through double, long and curly coats. Use light strokes; slicker pins can scratch skin if pressed hard.
  • Wide-tooth steel comb — the quality-check tool after brushing
  • Fine-tooth comb — for the face area
  • Dog-safe detangling spray
    One option: Chris Christensen Ice on Ice Detangling Spray (16 oz) on Amazon. A leave-in detangling spray with sunscreen, misted on before brushing so the pins slide through the coat instead of tearing it. Mist the coat lightly, not the skin; it's a finishing spray, not a substitute for a bath.
  • Dog-safe shampoo and conditioner appropriate for long coats
  • Pet-safe grooming wipes or saline solution for daily eye cleaning
  • Small nail clippers or file (or plan for monthly professional nail trims)
  • High-value training treats
    One option: Blue Buffalo Bits Soft Training Treats, Beef (19 oz) on Amazon. Soft, bite-size training treats with real beef as the first ingredient, small enough for rapid repetitions. Keep treats to about 10% of daily calories.
  • Appropriately sized toys — durable chews, puzzle toys, stuffed Kongs
  • Enzymatic cleaner
    One option: Rocco & Roxie Enzyme Stain & Odor Eliminator (32 oz) on Amazon. An enzyme stain and odor eliminator for urine, feces and vomit, carrying the Carpet and Rug Institute's seal for carpets. Spot-test on delicate fabrics first.

Establish the Grooming Routine Immediately

Lhasa Apso puppies have softer, more manageable coats than adults — this is the window to build grooming tolerance before the full adult coat arrives. Start brush sessions from day one, even if they're only 2–3 minutes. Touch every part of the body: paws, ears, inside the mouth, under the armpits. An adult Lhasa that accepts grooming without drama developed that tolerance as a puppy.

care.label: Renal Dysplasia Monitoring
care.heading: What should the first week with a Lhasa Apso puppy look like?
care.html:
What Is Renal Dysplasia?

Renal dysplasia is a progressive kidney disease that occurs at a meaningfully higher rate in Lhasa Apsos than in most breeds. It involves abnormal kidney development that progressively worsens. Some dogs show signs in puppyhood or young adulthood; others develop symptoms gradually over years. There is no cure — management focuses on supportive diet and veterinary care to slow progression and maintain quality of life.

Establishing Monitoring With Your Vet

At your first vet visit, raise renal dysplasia specifically. Ask your vet to:

  • Note baseline kidney values on the puppy's first blood panel (BUN, creatinine, phosphorus)
  • Establish a monitoring schedule — annual bloodwork that includes kidney values is the standard recommendation for this breed
  • Discuss early signs to watch for at home: increased water consumption, increased urination, weight loss, decreased appetite, lethargy

The goal is to catch any kidney function change early, when dietary and supportive management has the most impact.

Early Signs to Watch For

  • Drinking more water than usual (polydipsia)
  • Urinating more than usual, including overnight accidents in a housetrained dog
  • Unexplained weight loss despite normal or increased appetite
  • Decreased appetite or vomiting
  • General lethargy or reduced interest in activity

These signs can appear in young dogs (under 2 years) with early renal dysplasia, not just older dogs. If any appear, request kidney function bloodwork rather than assuming it's something else.

Pet Insurance Timing

Get pet insurance before the first vet visit — ideally before you pick up the puppy. The moment a vet records any observation in the medical record, there is a risk of that observation being used to exclude related conditions as pre-existing. Renal dysplasia coverage requires that no kidney concerns are documented before enrollment. Enroll the day you take ownership.

special.label: Socialization and Training
special.heading: Socializing an Independent Breed
special.html:
First Vet Visit (Within 48–72 Hours)

  • Full physical exam including eye exam (check for early signs of any eye issues) and patellar evaluation
  • Vaccine schedule verification
  • Discuss kidney monitoring plan with your vet
  • Parasite prevention
  • Microchip if not done by breeder
  • Discuss spay/neuter timing appropriate for a small breed

Socialization: Critical but Must Be Respected

Lhasa Apsos are naturally aloof with strangers — bred to be selective about who they trust. Socialization during the 8–16 week window doesn't make them universally friendly, but it does build confidence and reduces the risk that natural aloofness becomes anxiety or snappiness. The goal is a dog that is calm and controlled around strangers, not one that greets everyone enthusiastically.

  • Controlled, positive exposures to different people — don't force greetings, let the puppy approach when ready
  • Different environments: varied surfaces, sounds, settings
  • Teach the puppy that strangers mean good things (treat = person appears), not that strangers demand interaction
  • Carry the puppy in areas of disease risk rather than missing the socialization window

Training an Independent Thinker

Lhasa Apsos are capable of learning, but they're not motivated by pleasing you in the way a retriever is. What works: short sessions, high-value rewards, consistency. What doesn't: long repetitive drills, harsh corrections, expecting compliance every time regardless of context.

  • Crate training from day one — Lhasas generally adapt well to crates with patient introduction
  • Housetraining: consistent schedule, immediate reward for outdoor elimination, crate when unsupervised. Expect it to take longer than with more biddable breeds — 4–6 months of consistent work is typical
  • Basic commands: sit, stay, come, leave it — worth investing in, especially come and leave it for safety

Managing the Aloof Temperament Around Children

If you have children, teach them how to interact with the Lhasa from the start: no picking up uninvited, no grabbing, no approaching while the dog is eating or sleeping. The Lhasa's independence means it will communicate discomfort clearly — manage the environment so it doesn't need to. A dog that is never forced into overwhelming situations is a dog that doesn't learn that its only option is to snap.

faq.q: When should I find a groomer for my Lhasa Apso puppy?
faq.a: Find one before the puppy arrives, or within the first two weeks. The puppy's first professional grooming appointment — for a bath, blow-dry, and light tidy — can happen as early as 10–12 weeks (after initial vaccines). This early exposure makes the grooming process familiar rather than frightening. A puppy that has been groomed at 10, 14, and 18 weeks has a very different relationship with grooming than one who first encounters it at 6 months.

faq.q: Does renal dysplasia always appear in Lhasa Apsos?
faq.a: No — not all Lhasa Apsos develop it. But the breed is at meaningfully higher risk than most, and responsible breeders work to reduce the incidence in their lines. Asking breeders about kidney health history in their dogs is worthwhile, and establishing baseline kidney monitoring with your vet from puppyhood is the responsible owner approach regardless of what the breeder says.

faq.q: Are Lhasa Apsos easy to housetrain?
faq.a: Not especially. The independent, self-directed personality that makes Lhasas interesting companions also makes housetraining a patience exercise. Consistent schedule, crate training to prevent accidents when unsupervised, and immediate reward for outdoor elimination are the tools. Expect 4–6 months of consistent work rather than the 8-week timeline owners of more biddable breeds sometimes achieve. The key is never getting frustrated — Lhasas shut down with harsh correction, which makes progress slower, not faster.
